content.title: About
content.content: Pie with coconut cream is a dessert consisting of a tender crust and a silky filling made from coconut milk and shredded coconut. The coconut cream gives a distinctive aroma and light sweetness, while the crust can be shortbread, sponge, or puff pastry.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coconut cream is produced by blending coconut flesh with a small amount of water.
Traditionally these pies are made in tropical regions where coconut is a staple ingredient.
Coconut cream can replace dairy cream in vegan recipes.
The combination of a crunchy crust and creamy filling makes the pie popular in cafés and bakeries.
In some countries the pie is served with fruit sauces such as mango or pineapple.

items.title: Rich in healthy fats
items.content: Coconut cream contains medium‑chain triglycerides that are quickly metabolized and can provide rapid energy.

items.title: Source of iron and copper
items.content: The shredded coconut in the cream supplies trace minerals important for blood formation.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Coconut cream provides a modest amount of dietary fiber that helps maintain regular bowel movements.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Coconut cream is rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Suitable for people with lactose intolerance as it is entirely plant‑based.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut products.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Coconut cream is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑watching diets.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Although medium‑chain fats are metabolized quickly, they are still saturated, so people with cardiovascular concerns should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pie chilled or slightly warmed. It pairs well with berries, fruit sauces, or ice cream. Store leftover slices in the refrigerator for up to 3 days.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the pie in an airtight container in the fridge. For longer storage (up to 1 month) it can be frozen, preferably pre‑cut into serving portions.

potato-boiled-from-fresh-peel-eaten-fat-.title: Boiled Potato, fresh, peel eaten, with added fat, NS as fat type

content.title: About
content.content: Boiled potato is a product obtained by cooking fresh tubers in salted water. The peel is left on, increasing dietary fiber content. A small amount of vegetable fat (type NS – non‑specific) is added to the dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potato is the fourth most produced food crop worldwide.
The edible peel contains almost twice the fiber of the flesh.
Boiling preserves most of the vitamin C if not overcooked.
Adding a little fat improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins A and D.
Potatoes can be stored at +4 °C for several months.

items.title: Rich in carbohydrates
items.content: Provides complex carbs that supply steady energy without rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Supports immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Fiber in the peel
items.content: Aids digestive health and helps lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Regulates fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Fat enhances vitamin bioavailability
items.content: Vegetable fat helps the body absorb vitamins A and D more efficiently.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to potato.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt should be considered, especially for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Boiled potatoes have a high GI, which can raise blood sugar quickly.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Prolonged boiling can produce small amounts of acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve as a side dish, dice into salads, mash, or bake with vegetables. Rinse the peel well before boiling. Add 1‑2 tsp of vegetable oil to improve flavor and vitamin absorption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep boiled potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Longer storage may lead to soft texture and loss of flavor.

potato-roasted-from-fresh-peel-eaten-mad.title: Potato, roasted, from fresh, peel eaten, made with margarine

content.title: About
content.content: Roasted potato made from fresh tubers and cooked with margarine retains its natural flavor and aroma. The peel is eaten, preserving additional nutrients and fiber. It is a popular side dish and a standalone meal, commonly served in restaurants and home kitchens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Roasting gives potatoes a crispy crust and a golden color.
The peel contains more fiber, vitamins, and minerals than the flesh.
Margarine is used as a more affordable alternative to butter, adding a subtle richness.
Roasted potatoes are often served with a variety of sauces: ketchup, mayo, sour cream, or herb sauces.
In many cultures, roasted potatoes are a traditional dish for holidays and family gatherings.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C helps strengthen the immune system and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Fiber in the peel
items.content: Eating the peel increases dietary fiber intake, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Starch carbohydrates are rapidly converted to glucose, providing fast energy.

items.title: Antioxidants present
items.content: Potatoes contain phenolic compounds that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Roasting in margarine adds calories, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some margarines may contain trans fats, which are detrimental to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature roasting can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen.

items.title: Margarine allergy
items.content: Individuals sensitive to plant oils may experience allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted potatoes are served hot as a side dish, cut into slices, wedges, or cubes. They can be seasoned with salt, spices, herbs, or cheese. The peel is edible and nutritious, so no need to peel.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked roasted potatoes in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat in the oven or skillet to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: The dried vegetable mixture is made from finely ground dried vegetables such as carrot, onion, pepper, celery and others. The vegetables are blanched, sliced and dried at low temperature, preserving most of their nutrients and aromas. The blend is convenient, does not require refrigeration and is ideal for quick meal preparation.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dried vegetable mixes are popular in backpacking meals and vegetarian cooking.
A single blend can contain up to ten different vegetables, providing a broad spectrum of vitamins and minerals.
Low‑temperature drying retains up to 80 % of the original vitamin C content.
The mixture easily dissolves in hot water, creating a flavorful broth.
Manufacturers often add herbs such as parsley or basil to enhance taste.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vegetables provide B1, B2, B3 and B6 vitamins that support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Drying preserves most of the plant fiber, which aids normal digestion.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The blend contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Carotenoids and polyphenols that survive the drying process help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports immunity
items.content: Vitamin C and other micronutrients contribute to a healthy immune system.

items.title: Allergy to specific vegetables
items.content: People allergic to certain vegetables (e.g., onion) may react to the blend.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some mixes are fortified with salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Loss of heat‑sensitive vitamins
items.content: Heat during drying can reduce levels of vitamins such as vitamin C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add the dried vegetable mixture to soups, sauces, stews, porridge, or simply pour hot water over it to make a flavorful broth. It can serve as a base for vegetarian patties or casseroles. For extra depth, briefly toast the mixture in a dry pan before using.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage (over 6 months) keep it in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation and flavor loss.
